Mark Twain. Born Samuel Clemens in Hannibal, Missouri, and living from eighteen thirty-five to nineteen ten, he was the preeminent American humorist and satirist of the nineteenth century. A riverboat pilot turned journalist and novelist, he transmuted frontier experience and vernacular speech into fiction of enduring power and social critique. The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn are canonical American novels, and his wit and skepticism of authority shaped American literary voice.

He grew up in Hannibal on the Mississippi River, which became the setting and spiritual center of his greatest fiction. He worked as a riverboat pilot in his twenties. He took the pen name "Mark Twain," a riverboat term for safe water depth, as a journalist in Nevada and California during the eighteen sixties. The Innocents Abroad, published in eighteen sixty-nine, is a travel memoir satirizing American tourism and European pretension that became a bestseller and established his reputation. The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, published in eighteen seventy-six, presents a boy's adventures in Hannibal with nostalgia, humor, and moral complexity. It remains widely read as a children's classic. The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, published in eighteen eighty-four, is narrated by illiterate Huck, who escapes slavery to help the runaway slave Jim. It is often considered the greatest American novel, though it is now debated for its use of racial slurs and its equivocal treatment of racism.

A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court, published in eighteen eighty-nine, is a satire of chivalry and technological superiority, with American pragmatism encountering medieval romance. Twain was a master of vernacular speech and first-person narration. His use of authentic American dialects and colloquialism broke with genteel literary tradition. Through The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, which is a picaresque journey down the Mississippi between slavery and freedom, Twain created the archetypal American boyhood narrative with Tom Sawyer, establishing both works as foundational to American literature. His work captures the spirit and mythology of westward expansion and river culture. He established the vernacular humorist as a major American literary voice and helped define the coming-of-age novel form.
